content: Healthcare providers should avoid using a universal screening approach, such as standardized tools or criteria applied to all children during healthcare encounters, to identify potential child maltreatment. This recommendation is based on the 2019 WHO guidelines for the health sector response to child maltreatment. Instead, alternative evidence-based interventions should be considered to address child maltreatment, as outlined in the WHO technical report. For further details, refer to Box 9 of the guidelines. The WHO guideline on school health services (SHS) is part of a broader effort to provide global guidance on school health. It emphasizes the implementation of comprehensive SHS, supported by strong evidence of their effectiveness and acceptability. The guideline includes a list of 87 recommended interventions for SHS, along with supporting evidence, and identifies seven interventions deemed unsuitable for inclusion. While the guideline offers general advice on prioritizing interventions, further guidance on national SHS strategies, implementation, and monitoring is expected in the future. Monitoring and evaluation are integral to the implementation of the WHO guideline on SHS. These processes aim to assess effectiveness, document lessons learned, and guide future implementation. WHO plans to use the periodic Global Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health Policy Survey, conducted every 2–3 years, to evaluate the inclusion of SHS recommendations in national policies. Additional surveys will assess SHS integration into curricula and training programs. WHO will collaborate with national authorities to gather feedback on the implementation of SHS recommendations, including the experiences of educators, health staff, and community members. Progress and barriers to implementation will be tracked. WHO and UNESCO have developed global standards and indicators for health-promoting schools and systems. One of the eight standards relates to SHS, and specific monitoring and evaluation tools have been suggested. For more in-depth guidance on evidence-based interventions, a selection of WHO resources is available, including guidelines on topics such as tobacco control, adolescent reproductive health, pain management in children, and the treatment of severe acute malnutrition. Research is needed to address gaps in knowledge related to SHS governance, organization, standards of care, delivery modes, and effectiveness outcomes. This includes evaluating the outcomes of different governance models, health worker qualifications, and team compositions. Research should also explore how to meet the health needs of disadvantaged children and adolescents, including those out of school, with a focus on quality, coverage, and equity. Further research is required on the acceptability of SHS, including qualitative studies on student and family satisfaction, participatory research with young people, and differentiation of outcomes by sex and age. Additionally, cost-effectiveness studies are needed to determine the minimal investment required to maximize SHS effects. The WHO guideline on SHS will be updated as new evidence emerges. The Steering Group, in consultation with technical experts, will monitor developments in SHS research, particularly in areas where the certainty of existing evidence is low. Implementation research is also needed to improve SHS leadership, assess training fidelity, and adapt SHS during crises, such as through telemedicine during epidemics. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), controlled or prospective studies are required to evaluate SHS in diverse cultural settings, such as sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Case studies from various countries across WHO regions will also contribute to understanding SHS implementation. Innovation in SHS should be explored, including telehealth technologies and low-cost options like task-sharing and mobile clinics. These approaches could enhance access to care, particularly for remote or underserved populations.
